passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Silk Road Commercial Exchange

A The Silk Road denotes overlapping caravan and maritime routes linking East Asian production centres with Mediterranean consumers across two millennia, exchanging silk, spices, precious metals, and ideas rather than forming a single paved highway. Nomadic intermediaries controlled steppe segments, taxing caravans and supplying horses essential for desert crossings. Urban entrepôts such as Samarkand prospered on warehousing, money-changing, and craft specialisation serving transient merchants speaking multiple tongues. Historians caution against romanticising peaceful trade alone; military campaigns and epidemic transmissions accompanied commercial flows reshaping empires as much as luxury demand for patterned textiles did in courts far from weaving workshops.

B Han dynasty diplomatic missions established relationships facilitating silk exports toward Central Asia, while Roman elites paid premium prices for translucent fabrics mistaken as vegetable fibre rather than insect cocoon threads. Parthian empires intermediated to obscure direct contact, preserving markup chains. Archaeological finds in desert oases preserve documents in Sogdian script detailing loans, disputes, and family letters revealing everyday commercial anxieties beyond imperial annals. Shipwrecks along Indian Ocean routes carry ceramic cargoes tracing modularity of exchange where bulk goods moved by sea while high-value items crossed mountains on pack animals subject to banditry and seasonal snow closures.

C Buddhism, Manichaeism, and later Islam spread along trader networks, translating scriptures in monasteries adjoining bazaars where spiritual and material economies intertwined. Astronomy and papermaking technologies diffused unevenly, adapted to local materials and political patronage. Syncretic art styles blended motifs on metalwork sold to pilgrims and merchants alike. Scholars debate diffusionism versus independent invention when similar techniques appear distant chronologically; genetic and isotopic analyses of textiles now complement textual evidence, clarifying provenance of fibres and dyes traded over thousands of kilometres through relay systems rather than single merchant journeys end to end annually. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

D State policies alternately encouraged and restricted movement: Tang tolls and passport systems regulated foreigners in Chang'an quarters, while Mongol unification under the Pax Mongolica temporarily reduced fragmentation, lowering transaction costs across Eurasia. Maritime policies during Ming eras shifted emphasis to naval expeditions and then inward focus, altering spice flows through Southeast Asian ports competing for Arab and Gujarati shipping expertise. Tax farming on customs revenue incentivised officials to stimulate volume while courting corruption risks. Currency debasement in distant capitals nonetheless disrupted trust in copper coins used to settle caravan accounts, demonstrating monetary links between unrelated regimes participating in shared commercial circuits spanning continents.

E Social structures positioned caravan leaders, camel breeders, and port pilots as skilled brokers whose knowledge constituted capital. Slave and indentured labour appeared in mining and plantation commodities feeding route demand, connecting Silk Road histories to Indian Ocean coercive trades often omitted in celebratory narratives. Women managed households during long absences and participated in textile production supplying export quality. Gender historians recover contracts showing female moneylenders in oasis towns, complicating assumptions that long-distance trade was exclusively male public sphere activity devoid of kinship credit networks sustaining multi-generational firms branding reputation across deserts as valuable as silver ingots stamped with sovereign seals verifying weight purity.

F Decline narratives attributing route obsolescence solely to European oceanic circumnavigation oversimplify persistent overland segments feeding regional markets. Russian expansion and Qing consolidation reshaped northern corridors; simultaneously, new world silver influx altered price structures globally. European joint-stock companies integrated Asian goods into Atlantic consumption, yet Ottoman and Safavid realms remained vital intermediaries for centuries. Environmental historians note deforestation around oasis cities from fuel and construction demands, contributing to sand encroachment undermining habitation supporting relay stations essential when water management faltered, showing ecological limits intersecting with political fragmentation after plague depopulation events recalibrating labour availability and risk premiums charged by insurers emerging in Italian city-states.

G Looking ahead, modern belt-style infrastructure revivals invite comparison with ancient networks, risking anachronism if contemporary geopolitics are projected backward uncritically. The author argues studying the Silk Road clarifies how commerce coevolved with religion, disease, and statecraft rather than operating in economic isolation. Museums displaying silks should contextualise labour and coercion alongside aesthetic admiration. Responsible public history acknowledges plural actors—Sogdian, Persian, Chinese, East African—whose interactions forged a connected premodern world whose legacies inform today's debates about openness, security, and the price of interdependence along revived rail and port investments spanning the same geography with new energy commodities replacing spices as strategic priorities for great powers.
